beats.trigger: ## Security
beats.got: nothing new

beats.trigger: You can't tell if your agent is safe from its output. You need a check.
beats.got: Looking at the output won't show whether an agent is safe, so there has to be a separate check. That is at least honest.

beats.trigger: Read the [Agent Trigger List, After Module 3]
beats.got: nothing new. It is homework I haven't done, and it points to pages I can't see.

beats.trigger: **Apply** named agent risk patterns (direct and indirect prompt injection, secrets in context, tool confusion, skill supply chain)
beats.got: It is a list of jargon. I can't tell which items affect my money.

beats.trigger: Name what you'd want to check before letting this near a real stakeholder.
beats.got: I'm supposed to name checks, but I don't know what the thing is yet.

beats.trigger: Each tool has a name, a description and an input format.
beats.got: The agent writes text and a program turns it into actions. That is more mechanism than I need.

beats.trigger: Would you bet your job on it being safe?
beats.got: nothing new. It is dramatic, and it is not a figure.

beats.trigger: same input, same output.
beats.got: Normal software is predictable, so you can test it once and trust it.

beats.trigger: One passing test is one sample.
beats.got: Agents give different answers each time, so one clean test proves little. That is a real audit problem. Also, a document the agent reads can talk it into doing something.

beats.trigger: Scope (give the agent less). Split (two agents, different trust levels). Filter (post-process output). Gate (human approves). Review (a second agent judges).
beats.got: There are five concrete levers, and a human approval gate is the one I recognise as a control.

beats.trigger: *the residual risk is X; if Y happens, we made it less likely, not prevented it.*
beats.got: You write down what risk is left and sign for it. That is how I already treat risk, so it is usable.

beats.trigger: More context makes a good answer likelier. Less access makes a bad answer smaller.
beats.got: Less access means a smaller worst case. Scope it too far and it is useless.

beats.trigger: Expect it to cost you a feature.
beats.got: The cheapest control is not connecting the system at all, and it has a cost. It is the first time this module states a trade-off.

beats.trigger: Damn, this is complex stuff.
beats.got: nothing new. It repeats the loop and ends on a sentiment instead of a figure.

beats.trigger: A **skill** packages an expertise (rules, checklists, the moves an agent runs) into something the agent loads when the work matches.
beats.got: A skill is a saved, reusable checklist the agent loads. That is something I can picture.

beats.trigger: they show which rules files can check and which need judgment, context, or a standing evidence check.
beats.got: The agent sorts the policy rules into checkable and not checkable. I would want to see the actual rows, and the page doesn't show them.

beats.trigger: the customer your CEO would not want named in a transcript.
beats.got: I'm to type a few lines about what matters to my company. It is generic, and I don't have a finance example in front of me.

beats.trigger: Expect many questions; the agent keeps probing both lenses over several rounds.
beats.got: It takes 22 minutes of Q&A, and I can't see what it costs.

beats.trigger: *"You choose. Optimise for what I can't steer."*
beats.got: I can hand questions back to the agent, which suits me. I'd still be accepting its judgement on my company's policy.

beats.trigger: Run `ls .claude/skills/agent-audit/` to confirm.
beats.got: The check gets saved as files in a folder. This is the part I would hand to my controller or IT.

beats.trigger: Agent mitigations sit on top of normal company controls, not in place of them.
beats.got: The agent check is added to the controls we already have and doesn't replace them. That answers the question I would have raised.

beats.trigger: The goal is the loop (assess, mitigate, reassess residual), not a clean bill of health.
beats.got: The aim is to run the loop, not to get a pass. Fine, but I wanted a verdict.

beats.trigger: Type `/` and look for `/agent-audit` in the autocomplete list.
beats.got: You type a slash command to call the saved check.

beats.trigger: Expect the reusable check to find things you did not think about, and to leave things "I can't tell" you thought were settled.
beats.got: The audit gives three lists, including 'can't tell', and I get a report file with flagged rows I can open and check. This is the first part that works on my own material.

beats.trigger: The uncomfortable feeling is the evidence.
beats.got: I get a ranked risk report. The line about feelings as evidence is what I don't accept. I want evidence I can check, not a feeling.

beats.trigger: The risk remains. That is expected. Name it, accept it on record, and stop there.
beats.got: I pick one risk, apply one control, and write down what is left and who accepted it. That is a normal risk-register entry.

beats.trigger: Bring the report, the files it quotes, the mitigation you applied, and the residual that remains.
beats.got: When unsure, take the evidence to legal, security or IT with a narrow question. This is how I'd do it anyway, and it is good that the module says so.

beats.trigger: Risk control, done for every risk you found, separates a prototype from a production agent.
beats.got: We fixed one risk, and a production agent needs every one fixed. That is a hidden cost, and the page gives no size for it.

beats.trigger: The reusable check is the expert in the room, and it carries to the next agent.
beats.got: The saved check is reusable on the next agent, and the report keeps the evidence and decisions. That is something I could point the board at.

beats.trigger: The unease stays.
beats.got: The agent adds a few rules to the instructions file from the session. Fine, but 'the unease stays' is not a deliverable.

beats.trigger: A skill is not a deployed service and does not settle ownership.
beats.got: Skills can be built for other recurring jobs and given to a colleague, but sharing a file doesn't make anyone responsible for it. The module is honest about that.

beats.trigger: "I can't tell" is a real answer.
beats.got: nothing new, but it is a clean summary I could keep.

beats.trigger: Without the two sentences, you'll be writing them while the rest of the room is already comparing detectors. Your call.
beats.got: There is homework, and it is phrased as a mild threat.

beats.trigger: Read Mata v. Avianca (2023) and Deloitte Australia / DEWR report (2025) in the lecture.
beats.got: Two real cases of what happens when nobody checks the agent's output. The Deloitte one is a consulting firm and a government client, so I'd read it.

take_homes: An agent's output can't show whether it is safe, and it answers differently each run. A clean test is one sample. Only a separate check, run again, tells you more.
Write down the risk that is left after a control, and who accepted it. Where I can't tell, I take the report to legal, security or IT with a narrow question.
The cheapest control is not connecting the system or giving write access. It costs a feature, and agent controls sit on top of our existing controls, not instead of them.

monday.move: Send IT and my controller three questions about the tool for finance data: what can it read, what can it change, what must a person approve. Ask for the answers in writing before the month-end variance trial.
monday.who: Me, then IT and the controller
monday.stop_condition: If IT can't answer all three in writing, no finance data goes into any agent.
monday.blocker: IT has not approved the tool for finance data.

misconception.why: I came thinking AI is a licence you buy. The saved check carries our policy and the judgement about our system, and the module says it sits on top of our own controls. I didn't expect that, so it is more than a licence. I still can't say what it costs per month for 40 people, and nothing here told me.

one_line: The risk loop is sensible and I'd use it, but I got no cost or payback figure, and the 'unease is evidence' line isn't something I can put in front of a board.
